DoclingBackend's own per-page result cache (_page_cache, docling_backend.py) is a BOUNDED OrderedDict, max size 8, LRU eviction -- ruled out as an unbounded per-page accumulation source (source-verified, not assumed).
No child/worker processes exist for either extraction process at any point checked (ps --ppid / pgrep -P both empty) -- ruled out multiprocessing/subprocess amplification as the mechanism.

_get_component_backends() caches one Docling instance + one Table Transformer instance per (device, ocr_languages, ocr_backend) key for the PROCESS LIFETIME (src/doc_extraction/cli.py) -- a deliberate, documented design choice to avoid reloading model weights per page; this guarantees a persistent baseline RSS floor from loaded model weights, by design, for the life of the process.
probable: Two concurrent worker processes, each independently holding this per-process model-weight floor plus their own working-set churn, combined to exceed system RAM (31GB, 0 swap) when running together -- consistent with chunk1's RSS trending DOWN (11.8GB peak while concurrent -> 8-9GB range once alone) once chunk0's contention was removed.

No explicit gc.collect() or cache-clearing call exists anywhere in this project's own pipeline code between pages (grep-verified) -- Python/PyTorch's own CPU allocator is known to retain freed memory in its own arena pool rather than returning it to the OS promptly, which is a plausible contributor to the oscillating-but-occasionally-spiking RSS pattern observed, though this is a property of the underlying allocator, not a defect in this project's code.
unresolved: Whether a SINGLE isolated worker, run alone with no concurrent second process, can independently reach the 12GB+ danger zone given enough pages/complexity -- not yet observed either way; this is exactly what the Phase F calibration test (in progress) is measuring.

Whether any specific page (e.g. an unusually large or dense image) causes a disproportionate one-time memory spike vs. gradual accumulation across many pages -- the calibration test's size-diverse page selection is designed to surface this if present, but 4 pages is not enough to rule it out definitively.

concurrency_hypothesis_finalized.supported: Concurrent heavy extraction increases aggregate memory pressure sufficiently to trigger global OOM. Evidence: (1) original two-worker run -> chunk0 killed at 12.1GB anon-RSS while chunk1 concurrently held ~8-10GB, combined exceeding 31GB/0-swap; (2) chunk1 running ALONE (no competing recovery worker) subsequently reached ~12.9GB anon-RSS -- EXCEEDING chunk0's exact kill value -- and returned to its normal band WITHOUT any OOM, confirmed via journalctl -k showing no kill event; (3) batch0 (single recovery worker) + chunk1 running concurrently produced 3 low-available-memory alerts (min 2476MB) that chunk1-alone conditions have not reproduced; (4) batch0 alone-style (one recovery worker, chunk1 as the only other heavy process) completed 20/20 pages with peak 10.07GB, no OOM.
concurrency_hypothesis_finalized.not_proven: Do NOT claim: (a) one worker is universally memory-safe indefinitely -- not tested at length beyond chunk1's own 76+ pages and batch0's 20 pages; (b) memory growth is 'solved' -- the spike-and-release mechanism itself remains uncharacterized at the allocator level; (c) any specific RSS number (12.1GB, 12.9GB) is a safe or unsafe per-process ceiling -- both observations are population/timing-dependent, not fixed thresholds.
concurrency_hypothesis_finalized.conclusion: Single-worker/process-recycled execution is materially safer than concurrent heavy workers under this 31GB/no-swap environment. This is a narrower, evidence-scoped claim, not a general memory-safety proof.
concurrency_hypothesis_finalized.operating_rule: Use system-wide AVAILABLE memory and observed behavior as the operating signal, never a specific historical per-process RSS number (neither 12.1GB nor 12.9GB) as a threshold.
